newsitem.title: UK: Rover eyes higher sales in 97, still sees losses.
newsitem.headline: Rover eyes higher sales in 97, still sees losses.

text.p: German owned Rover group, the British car maker, predicted that 1997 sales would rise even though the group would likely not swing to profit before the end of the decade.
Rover chief executive Walter Hasselkus told German journalists on Thursday that he expected turnover to climb this year, but added that demand in Britain would stagnate.
A source close to Rover said 1996 sales should be around 16 billion marks ($9.5 billion), up from 13 billion marks reported in 1995.
Last year Rover sales totalled more than 500,000 vehicles, for the first time since 1988, the group said in late January.
Rover is owned by German car maker BMW.
Higher demand, improved currency market conditions and a better product mix all contributed to higher sales, Hasselkus said, adding that the group had invested over seven percent of the 1996 sales.

Hasselkus however declined to be drawn out on the group's results referring only to BMW chief Bernd Pischetsrieder's comments from last year that Rover's 1995 pre-tax loss of 335 million marks was already the highest that was expected.
He did however confirm that Rover would not move into the black until the end of the decade.

Hasselkus assured that BMW's investments in Rover were of a serious nature and that Rover's three U.K. plants would still be operating in the 10 years. "The Rover cars will become even more British in their character," Hasselkus said.
Turning to the group's marketing plans, Hasselkus said BMW and Rover would join sales forces in non-key markets but keep their sales operations separate in key markets like Germany.

Hasselkus said that synergies from the merger had not yet been fully realised and that there was still savings potential totalling some several hundred million marks. The biggest savings could be realised in purchasing, Hasselkus said.
